questions.q: Which description best fits the greedy algorithm design paradigm?
choices: Build a solution step by step, making the choice that looks best at each step
Split the problem into subproblems, solve them, and combine their answers
Check every possible solution and keep the best one
Start from any solution and keep improving it until nothing gets better
questions.explain: A greedy algorithm builds a solution iteratively through a sequence of locally appealing decisions. Splitting, solving, and combining is divide and conquer.

questions.q: Greedy decisions are called myopic because each one picks whatever looks best right now without explicitly considering all of its later consequences.
questions.explain: Myopic means short-sighted. Each greedy choice optimizes the current step only.

questions.q: For a typical greedy algorithm, which part is usually the hardest?
choices: Proving that the local rule always gives a globally optimal solution
Coming up with a plausible local rule
Analyzing the running time
Writing the pseudocode
questions.explain: Greedy rules are usually easy to propose, and their running time is usually easy to analyze. Correctness is the hard part.

questions.q: If a greedy algorithm runs in O(n log n) time, it must produce an optimal solution.
questions.explain: Running time and correctness are separate questions. The difference rule sorts just as fast as the ratio rule, but it can return a suboptimal schedule.

questions.q: Which statements about evaluating a proposed greedy rule are true?
choices: A single counterexample is enough to show the rule is incorrect
Many examples where the rule works prove that it is correct
A proof such as an exchange argument can show the rule is correct
Most plausible greedy rules are guaranteed to be correct
questions.explain: One counterexample disproves a rule, but no number of successful examples proves it. Correctness needs a proof. Most plausible greedy rules are not correct.

questions.q: Which of these describes divide and conquer rather than greedy?
choices: Split the problem into smaller subproblems, solve them, and combine their answers
Make one locally best decision after another
Give each item a priority, sort by it, and process items in that order
Commit to each choice without considering all of its later consequences
questions.explain: Divide, conquer, combine is the divide-and-conquer pattern. The other three describe greedy algorithms.

questions.q: How many different schedules (orderings) are there for 7 distinct jobs on one machine?
questions.explain: There are n! orderings of n jobs. 7! = 7·6·5·4·3·2·1 = 5040.

questions.q: What is the completion time C_j(σ) of job j in schedule σ?
choices: Its own length plus the lengths of all jobs scheduled before it
The total length of all jobs scheduled before it
Its own length times its weight
Its own length plus the lengths of all jobs scheduled after it
questions.explain: C_j(σ) = ℓ_j + (sum of ℓ_i for every i before j). It is the time job j finishes, not when it starts.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (2, 5), J2 = (4, 1), J3 = (3, 2). The schedule is (J2, J1, J3). What is the completion time of J1?
questions.explain: J2 runs first and finishes at 4. J1 runs next and finishes at 4 + 2 = 6.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (2, 5), J2 = (4, 1), J3 = (3, 2). What is the sum of weighted completion times Σ w_j·C_j for the schedule (J2, J1, J3)?
questions.explain: Completion times are C2 = 4, C1 = 6, C3 = 9. The sum is 1·4 + 5·6 + 2·9 = 4 + 30 + 18 = 52.

questions.q: In the single-machine weighted scheduling problem, what is the objective?
choices: Minimize the sum over all jobs of w_j·C_j(σ)
Minimize the sum over all jobs of C_j(σ), ignoring weights
Minimize the largest completion time
Maximize the sum over all jobs of w_j·C_j(σ)
questions.explain: We want the ordering σ that minimizes the sum of weighted completion times. A heavier job costs more for each unit of time it waits.

questions.q: Which assumptions belong to the scheduling model for which the ratio rule is proved optimal?
choices: One machine processes one job at a time
All jobs are available from the start
Once a job starts, it runs to completion without interruption
All lengths and weights are positive
Jobs may be paused and resumed later
Jobs arrive at different release times
questions.explain: The model has one machine, all jobs available at time 0, no interruption, and positive lengths and weights. Pausing jobs or staggered arrivals fall outside it.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (1, 3), J2 = (2, 2), J3 = (3, 1). What is Σ w_j·C_j for the schedule (J3, J2, J1)?
Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (1, 2), J2 = (3, 9). What is Σ w_j·C_j for the schedule that shortest job first produces?
questions.explain: Shortest first runs J1 then J2: C1 = 1, C2 = 4, so the cost is 2·1 + 9·4 = 38. Running J2 first gives 9·3 + 2·4 = 35, so shortest job first is not optimal here.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (8, 3), J2 = (2, 2). Which statement is true?
choices: Highest weight first costs 44, but running J2 first costs 34
Highest weight first costs 34 and is optimal
Both orders cost the same
Highest weight first costs 44 and is optimal
questions.explain: Highest weight first runs J1 then J2: 3·8 + 2·10 = 44. Running J2 first gives 2·2 + 3·10 = 34. Weight alone is not enough. Length matters too.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (10, 8), J2 = (2, 1). Which order does the difference rule (sort by w − ℓ, descending) choose, and what does it cost?
choices: J2 then J1, cost 98
J1 then J2, cost 92
J2 then J1, cost 92
J1 then J2, cost 98
questions.explain: The differences are J1: −2 and J2: −1, so J2 goes first. C2 = 2, C1 = 12, and the cost is 1·2 + 8·12 = 98. The ratio rule (0.8 > 0.5) puts J1 first and costs 8·10 + 1·12 = 92, which is better.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): J1 = (5, 3), J2 = (2, 1). What is Σ w_j·C_j for the schedule the difference rule (w − ℓ, descending) produces?
questions.explain: The differences are −2 for J1 and −1 for J2, so J2 goes first: C2 = 2, C1 = 7, and the cost is 1·2 + 3·7 = 23. The ratio rule puts J1 first and costs 3·5 + 1·7 = 22.

questions.q: If the ratio rule gives a lower cost than the difference rule on one instance, that proves the ratio rule is always optimal.
questions.explain: One instance can only disprove the difference rule. The ratio rule is proved optimal by the exchange argument.

questions.q: Sorting jobs in descending order of w_j/ℓ_j is equivalent to sorting them by:
choices: ℓ_j/w_j in ascending order
ℓ_j/w_j in descending order
w_j/ℓ_j in ascending order
w_j − ℓ_j in descending order
questions.explain: With positive values, a larger w/ℓ means a smaller ℓ/w. So descending w/ℓ is the same order as ascending ℓ/w.

questions.q: Consecutive jobs i and j start after T units of earlier work. Let A be the pair's cost with i first and B the cost with j first. What is A − B?
choices: w_j·ℓ_i − w_i·ℓ_j
w_i·ℓ_j − w_j·ℓ_i
w_i·ℓ_i − w_j·ℓ_j
T·(w_i − w_j) + w_j·ℓ_i − w_i·ℓ_j
questions.explain: A = w_i(T + ℓ_i) + w_j(T + ℓ_i + ℓ_j) and B = w_j(T + ℓ_j) + w_i(T + ℓ_j + ℓ_i). Everything cancels except w_j·ℓ_i − w_i·ℓ_j.

questions.q: In the exchange argument, how much work T comes before the pair can change whether i should go before j.
questions.explain: T appears as w_i·T + w_j·T in both A and B, so it cancels. The best order of two adjacent jobs depends only on their own lengths and weights.

questions.q: Why does swapping two adjacent jobs i and j leave the completion times of all later jobs unchanged?
choices: The pair finishes at T + ℓ_i + ℓ_j in either order
Later jobs always have smaller weights
A job's completion time depends only on its own length
Later jobs are already sorted by ratio
questions.explain: Both orders use the same total time, so every job after the pair starts and finishes at the same time either way.

questions.q: Putting adjacent job i before job j is at least as good as the reverse exactly when:
choices: w_i/ℓ_i ≥ w_j/ℓ_j
w_i/ℓ_i ≤ w_j/ℓ_j
w_i − ℓ_i ≥ w_j − ℓ_j
ℓ_i ≤ ℓ_j
questions.explain: A ≤ B iff w_j·ℓ_i ≤ w_i·ℓ_j iff w_i/ℓ_i ≥ w_j/ℓ_j.

questions.q: Adjacent jobs i = (ℓ = 3, w = 2) and j = (ℓ = 1, w = 4) start after T = 5 units of earlier work. With A = cost of the pair when i goes first and B = cost when j goes first, what is A − B?
questions.explain: A − B = w_j·ℓ_i − w_i·ℓ_j = 4·3 − 2·1 = 10. Directly: A = 2·8 + 4·9 = 52 and B = 4·6 + 2·9 = 42. Putting j first saves 10.

questions.q: If two adjacent jobs have equal ratios w/ℓ, swapping them leaves the total weighted completion time unchanged.
questions.explain: Equal ratios mean w_j·ℓ_i = w_i·ℓ_j, so A − B = 0. Ties can go in either order.

questions.q: The proof divides w_j·ℓ_i ≤ w_i·ℓ_j by ℓ_i·ℓ_j to get w_i/ℓ_i ≥ w_j/ℓ_j. Why doesn't this flip the inequality?
choices: Lengths are positive, so ℓ_i·ℓ_j > 0
Weights are integers
T cancels out of the difference
The two jobs are adjacent
questions.explain: Dividing by a positive number keeps the inequality's direction. This is one reason the model requires positive lengths.

questions.q: How does the exchange argument conclude that the ratio-sorted schedule is optimal?
choices: Swapping out-of-order adjacent pairs turns any schedule, even an optimal one, into the ratio-sorted schedule without ever raising the cost
It shows the ratio rule beats the difference rule on a counterexample
It checks all n! schedules and finds the sorted one is cheapest
It shows that every swap of two adjacent jobs strictly lowers the cost
questions.explain: Swapping an adjacent pair that is out of ratio order never increases the cost. Repeating this, as in bubble sort, turns an optimal schedule into the sorted one with no increase, so the sorted schedule is also optimal.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): P = (2, 6), Q = (6, 9), R = (3, 12), S = (4, 2). In what order does the ratio rule schedule them?
choices: R, P, Q, S
R, Q, P, S
P, R, S, Q
S, Q, P, R
questions.explain: The ratios w/ℓ are P = 3, Q = 1.5, R = 4, S = 0.5. Descending order is R, P, Q, S. (R, Q, P, S is highest weight first, P, R, S, Q is shortest first, and S, Q, P, R sorts the ratios the wrong way.)

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): P = (2, 6), Q = (6, 9), R = (3, 12), S = (4, 2). What is the minimum possible Σ w_j·C_j?
questions.explain: The ratio order is R, P, Q, S with completion times 3, 5, 11, 15. The cost is 12·3 + 6·5 + 9·11 + 2·15 = 36 + 30 + 99 + 30 = 195.

questions.q: What is the overall running time of the greedy ratio-rule scheduling algorithm on n jobs?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
O(n!)
questions.explain: Computing ratios is O(n), sorting is O(n log n), and computing completion times is O(n). Sorting dominates. Brute force over all n! orders would be far slower.

questions.q: Using integer cross-multiplication, which job has the higher ratio-rule priority: J_a = (ℓ = 5, w = 8) or J_b = (ℓ = 3, w = 5)?
choices: J_b, because w_b·ℓ_a = 25 > w_a·ℓ_b = 24
J_a, because w_a·ℓ_a = 40 > w_b·ℓ_b = 15
J_a, because its weight is larger
They tie
questions.explain: To compare w_a/ℓ_a with w_b/ℓ_b, compare w_a·ℓ_b = 8·3 = 24 with w_b·ℓ_a = 5·5 = 25. Since 24 < 25, 8/5 < 5/3, so J_b goes first.

questions.q: With integer lengths and weights, why compare w_i·ℓ_j with w_j·ℓ_i instead of computing w_i/ℓ_i and w_j/ℓ_j directly?
choices: It avoids floating-point rounding, as long as the integer type is wide enough not to overflow
It changes the asymptotic running time from O(n log n) to O(n)
It gives a different and better schedule than the ratio rule
Division by a length is undefined for integers
questions.explain: Cross-multiplication gives the same comparison using exact integer math. The products must fit in the integer type.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): X = (2, 4), Y = (3, 6), Z = (1, 5). Which schedules are optimal?
choices: Z, X, Y
Z, Y, X
X, Z, Y
X, Y, Z
questions.explain: The ratios are X = 2, Y = 2, Z = 5. Z goes first, and X and Y tie, so either order works. Both cost 53. X, Z, Y costs 59 and X, Y, Z costs 68.

questions.q: Jobs (length ℓ, weight w): X = (2, 4), Y = (3, 6), Z = (1, 5). What is the minimum possible Σ w_j·C_j?
questions.explain: Using Z, X, Y: C = 1, 3, 6, so the cost is 5·1 + 4·3 + 6·6 = 5 + 12 + 36 = 53. Z, Y, X gives 5 + 24 + 24 = 53 as well.

questions.q: Scheduling jobs in descending order of w_j/ℓ_j to minimize the sum of weighted completion times is commonly known as whose rule?
questions.explain: Sorting by descending weight-to-length ratio is called Smith's rule.
